title: Number of Ways to Assign Edge Weights I
statement:
A tree has `n` nodes labeled `1` to `n`, and node `1` is its root. The array `edges` holds its `n - 1` edges: `edges[i] = [u, v]` connects nodes `u` and `v`. Each edge can be given a weight of `1` or `2`, and the cost of a path is the sum of the weights of its edges.

Let `x` be a node whose depth (the number of edges between it and node `1`) is the largest in the tree; when several nodes share that depth, any of them may be used and the count below is the same. Looking only at the edges on the path from node `1` to `x`, count the ways to weight those edges so that the path's cost is odd. Return the count modulo `10^9 + 7`.
constraints: edges[i] == [u, v] with 1 <= u, v <= n
notes:
## Intuition

Only the path from node `1` to a deepest node counts, so the tree matters only through `maxDepth`, the number of edges on that path. A weight of `2` never changes whether a total is odd, so the cost is odd exactly when an odd number of the path's edges weigh `1`.

Trying all `2^maxDepth` assignments would be exponential, but there is a pairing: fix the weights of every edge except the first; then one of the two choices for the first edge makes the total odd and the other makes it even. So exactly half of all assignments are odd, and the answer is `2^(maxDepth - 1)`. It depends only on the depth, which is why any deepest node gives the same count. The only real work is a depth-first search for `maxDepth`.

## Approach

1. Build `adjacency`, the neighbours of every node, from the undirected edges.
2. Run an iterative DFS from node `1` with `stack`. A neighbour whose `depth` is still `-1` gets `depth[node] + 1` and is pushed; every popped node updates `maxDepth`.
3. Start `ways` at `1` and double it `maxDepth - 1` times, reducing modulo `MOD` each time.
4. Return `ways`, which is `2^(maxDepth - 1) mod (10^9 + 7)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`edges = [[1,2]]`, so `n = 2` and `adjacency[1] = [2]`, `adjacency[2] = [1]`. The DFS pops node `1` (depth `0`) and gives node `2` depth `1`; popping node `2` makes `maxDepth = 1`, and its neighbour `1` is already marked. The doubling loop runs `0` times, so the answer is `ways = 1`: only weight `1` makes the single edge odd. (In Example 2 nodes `4` and `5` reach depth `2`, so `ways` doubles once to `2`.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): the DFS handles each node and edge once, and the doubling loop runs fewer than `n` times.
- Space: O(n) for `adjacency`, `depth` and `stack`.

## Pitfalls

- An edge `[u, v]` does not say which end is the parent; the `depth[next] === -1` test stops the search from walking back up.
- The answer depends on the deepest node's depth, not on `n` or on how many deepest nodes there are.
- A recursive DFS on a path of `10^5` nodes can overflow the call stack; the explicit `stack` avoids that.
- `2^(maxDepth - 1)` is far too large for a number; reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` after every doubling.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `adjacency` | `adjacency[node]` lists the neighbours of `node` |
| `depth` | edges from node `1` to each node, `-1` while unreached |
| `stack` | nodes reached but not yet expanded |
| `node`, `next` | the node being expanded and one of its neighbours |
| `maxDepth` | largest depth seen, the number of edges on the chosen path |
| `ways` | assignments with an odd cost, `2^(maxDepth - 1)` modulo `MOD` |

narration.4: Make an empty neighbour list for every node label from 1 to n.
narration.5: Edges are undirected, so each one is recorded at both of its ends.
narration.10: No node has a depth yet; -1 marks a node as unreached.
narration.11: The root, node 1, is at depth 0.
narration.12: The depth-first search starts from the root.
narration.14: Keep going until every node has been expanded.
narration.15: Take the most recently found node.
narration.16: Its depth may be the largest seen so far.
narration.17: Look at each neighbour of this node.
narration.18: An unreached neighbour is a child: the parent already has a depth.
narration.19: A child sits one edge deeper than its parent.
narration.25: Start from 1: a path of one edge has exactly one odd weighting (weight 1).
narration.26: Half of the 2^maxDepth weightings are odd, so double maxDepth - 1 times.
narration.27: Double the count and reduce it modulo MOD so it stays small.
